question.text: If the mid-month USDINR futures has a higher premium than the near-month, this pattern is called:

explanation.text: The Logic: When a longer-dated futures contract trades at a higher price than a nearer-dated one, the futures curve is said to be in contango (also called a "normal market"). For USDINR, the cost-of-carry relationship makes contango the typical state: because INR interest rates are usually higher than USD rates, the no-arbitrage forward USDINR price rises with tenor. A mid-month USDINR futures priced above the near-month therefore reflects an upward-sloping, contango curve. The Trap: Backwardation is the opposite shape — near-month above far-month — which is unusual for USDINR. Arbitrage is a trading activity that exploits mispricings, not a label for a curve shape. Convergence refers to the futures price moving toward spot as expiry approaches, again not a description of the term structure shape itself. Note: The cited NISM Series I Currency Derivatives workbook pages reviewed in the audit support near/mid/far-month contract terminology and the interest-rate-differential explanation for USDINR futures premiums, but do not explicitly use the "contango / backwardation / normal market" labels on the pages checked. The framing above reflects general industry terminology for futures curve shapes.
